failure_summary.description: Answer echoed or restated the clue instead of the slot it asks for. This happened three ways: the named treaty was given when 'his' asks for the person; the parody form 'Oil's...' was given when the clue asks for the original title; and the clue's foreign word 'Ananas' was given when 'this tropical fruit' asks for the English name.
A bare two-name fragment ('Princess X & Princess Y') asks for the shared country or realm. The agent answered the relationship word 'sisters'.

The archive line and the flashcard both showed the bare surname as the answer. The agent expanded it to the full name, so the Rule 4 'natural name form' habit beat the Rule 3 verbatim-copy instruction.

patch.reasoning: Three of the five failures are the same kind of error: the answer reuses the clue's own subject, wording or language (the treaty named in the clue, the altered title, the foreign word). Each edit gives a concrete, checkable substitution for one of these cases: 'his/her' means the person, 'changed X to Y' means the original, and a foreign word in the clue means the English name. A fourth edit moves the shared-entity rule for name fragments into a prominent bullet and bans relationship words as answers. A fifth edit makes the Rule 3 verbatim-copy rule explicit that bare surnames stay bare. The edits are short and insert or replace at specific points, because earlier long 'Step 0' style insertions regressed the score. They avoid per-task facts, and the examples given are generic.

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- ECHO CHECK: the answer is never the clue's own subject or one of its own words. Three common cases:
  * A bare possessive or pronoun ('his final defeat', 'her debut', 'whose') after a named treaty, battle, work or event asks for the PERSON the pronoun refers to. The treaty or event is the anchor ('The 18xx Treaty of X was signed after his defeat...' -> the defeated leader, not the treaty).
  * A foreign-language word or dish/title name inside the clue ('Tarte au citron', 'Coupe a l'ananas') plus 'this fruit/animal/food/place' asks for the ENGLISH common name of that word (use the passage that glosses or translates it, and keep the plural for crops). The foreign word itself is wrong.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content: - ALTERED-TITLE clues ('a spoof changed "Moon" to "Mars" in this title', 'swapped one word in this phrase', 'a parody of this title') ask for the ORIGINAL, unaltered title or phrase, with the clue's changed word reversed. Passages mostly show the parody form; do not copy it. Write the standard original with its normal punctuation (apostrophes, commas).

edits.target: If the list is of real people, answer with the team, state or other entity they share.
edits.content: If the clue is a bare fragment naming two or more REAL people or things ('Princess A & Princess B', 'Senators X and Y', 'Players P, Q'), answer with the ONE proper noun they all share: the country or realm (for princes, princesses, kings, queens), state or city (for senators, governors, mayors), team, band or work. Relationship or category words ('sisters', 'brothers', 'royalty', 'family', 'politicians') are never the answer, and neither is one of the listed people. Pick the place or group that every passage pairs with every name, and give its bare common name.

edits.target: Before the answer tags, briefly quote the matched line.
edits.content: - The archived answer is final even when it is a bare surname or shorter than the natural full name: a line ending '| Lincoln.' or a flashcard 'CLUE TEXT, LINCOLN' gives 'Lincoln', never 'Abraham Lincoln'. Never add a first name, title or descriptor that the archive line does not show. Rule 4's 'natural name form' applies only when there is no archive answer. Look for archive-style passages (jeopardy dumps on GitHub, StudyStack flashcards, TriviaBistro, J! Archive) before choosing a form. A passage that repeats the clue with no answer after it is not a hit.
